main.title: Rave Racer
main.summary: Rave Racer is a 1995 racing video game developed and published by Namco for arcades.

cards.heading: A linked arcade grid
cards.text: Rave Racer is a 1995 racing video game developed and published by Namco for arcades. It is the third title in the Ridge Racer series and the follow-up to Ridge Racer and Ridge Racer 2. Rave Racer runs on Namco System 22 hardware, and could be played by two people per cabinet for up to eight players total when up to four of them were linked together.

cards.heading: New roads and a familiar drift
cards.text: Compared to Ridge Racer 2, Rave Racer adds two new tracks as well as the ability to play the original two, various handling changes, force feedback steering, and improved car and racetrack graphics. Rave Racer was a critical and commercial success; it would be the last major arcade Ridge Racer title until Ridge Racer V: Arcade Battle (2000) as Namco focused on home consoles with titles such as R4: Ridge Racer Type 4 (1998) and Ridge Racer 64 (2000).

main.title: Tekken 2
main.summary: Tekken 2 is a 1995 fighting game developed and published by Namco.

cards.text: Tekken 2 is a 1995 fighting game developed and published by Namco. The second entry in the Tekken series, it was released for arcades in August 1995, and was ported to the PlayStation in 1996. The home console version introduced new, now-staple game modes to the series, as well as full-motion video endings for every character. It was re-released as a playable game within Tekken 5 on PlayStation 2 (PS2) in 2005, digitally on PlayStation Network for PS3 and PSP in 2007, and on PlayStation Plus for PS4 and PS5 in 2023.

There are 25 playable fighters in the game, which includes 17 returning veterans from the original Tekken and eight newcomers, including Jun Kazama and Lei Wulong. The former boss, Heihachi Mishima, is now playable from the start as he seeks revenge in the plot, with Kazuya becoming the new antagonist. Tekken 2 was a critical as well as commercial success, with about 40,000 arcade units and 5.7 million PlayStation copies sold worldwide, and becoming one of the best-selling PlayStation games. Critics praised its graphical visuals and light sourcing, as well as its deep system of moves and combos, and the soundtrack. Tekken 2 was followed by a sequel, Tekken 3 (1997).

main.title: Puzzle Bobble
main.subtitle: Finding the angle
main.summary: On January 13, 1995, Puzzle Bobble reaches the Super Famicom in Japan, bringing home a formula Taito had introduced in arcades the previous year.

cards.heading: Bubbles reach the Super Famicom
cards.text: Puzzle Bobble reached Japan's Super Famicom on January 13, 1995, following Taito's arcade game of the previous year. Bub and Bob operate a launcher beneath a field of coloured bubbles. Connecting three or more of the same colour clears them, while the ceiling gradually descends. Players aim directly at a cluster or bounce shots off a side wall to reach a more difficult opening.

cards.heading: A clear field of play
cards.text: A launcher at the bottom and coloured clusters above make the arrangement easy to understand. Players can pause to judge the next trajectory, then watch how the bubble changes the field. Bub and Bob preserve a familiar link to Bubble Bobble, even though the action now depends on aiming, colour and distance. The home version makes the arcade challenge available for repeated practice.

cards.heading: Banking a shot
cards.text: The side walls let players bank shots around existing clusters. Removing bubbles can also separate a whole group from its support, clearing more of the field at once. An opening may be useful immediately or prepare a later shot. The remaining bubbles change the available angles after every move, combining careful aim with planning several steps ahead.

cards.heading: From Bubble Bobble to a new genre
cards.text: Taito describes Puzzle Bobble as a 1994 spin-off of Bubble Bobble and the origin of the bubble-shooter genre. It reused the recognisable bubble dragons around a new set of rules. The series eventually grew beyond twenty titles across consoles, computers and mobile devices, while its suspended field and colour-matching shots inspired many other games.

main.title: Ristar
main.summary: Ristar is a 1995 platform game developed and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis.

cards.text: Ristar is a 1995 platform game developed and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis. The game stars an anthropomorphic cartoon star who uses his hands and long, stretchable arms to both move and fight enemies. Reception for the game was generally positive, but the game's initial release was overshadowed due to the imminent ending of the Genesis's lifecycle and the succession of the Sega Saturn and other fifth generation video game consoles.

While never receiving any sequels, Sega has re-released Ristar several times digitally and on Sega-themed compilations, including the Sega Forever line of releases for mobile devices. The character has additionally received various cameos in other Sega properties as well. A Game Gear version of Ristar featured different level design and gameplay mechanics.

main.title: Alien Soldier
main.subtitle: The next boss is already waiting
main.summary: Treasure concentrates its Mega Drive action around formidable bosses and a versatile fighter with weapons, counters and a powerful dash.

cards.heading: Epsilon-Eagle
cards.text: Alien Soldier is Treasure’s single-player run-and-gun game, first released for Mega Drive in Japan on 24 February 1995. The player controls Epsilon-Eagle through short stretches of ordinary enemies that quickly lead to much larger opponents. Boss encounters form the centre of the game, with each creature demanding attention to its attacks and vulnerable moments. Six weapon types and several movement techniques give the player a substantial set of tools to learn. The challenge comes from choosing and executing the right response while the next pattern is already unfolding.

cards.heading: Choosing how to shoot
cards.text: Before starting, the player chooses four of the six weapons to carry. Each has its own ammunition reserve, making a change of gun part of managing a fight. One firing style permits movement while shooting; the other fixes Epsilon-Eagle in place for more precise aiming. Double jumping and hovering provide further ways to adjust position around a boss. A weapon’s reach matters together with the room available to stand, jump or stay airborne, so learning an encounter includes learning where each tool can be used safely.

cards.heading: Turning defence into an opening
cards.text: Epsilon-Eagle can counter enemy projectiles and turn them into health when the timing is right. At full health, his dash becomes the damaging Phoenix Force, joining survival and attack in a useful loop: recover, restore the stronger move and choose a moment to pass through the enemy. Hideyuki Suganami led development, with other Treasure staff helping bring the ambitious project to completion. Its late Mega Drive release reached North America through Sega Channel, while Japanese and European players could buy cartridges of this concentrated series of duels.

main.title: Lufia II: Rise of the Sinistrals
main.subtitle: Before the first adventure
main.summary: Lufia II: Rise of the Sinistrals is a Japanese role-playing game about Maxim and the companions who join his struggle against the Sinistrals. Released on the Super Nintendo, it takes place ninety-nine years before the first Lufia. That position gives the adventure a particular weight: it explores the people behind a history already introduced to players. Towns and turn-based battles supply a familiar framework, while the dungeons ask for observation and manipulation of the environment as well as a strong party.

cards.heading: Before the first adventure
cards.text: Lufia II: Rise of the Sinistrals is a Japanese role-playing game about Maxim and the companions who join his struggle against the Sinistrals. Released on the Super Nintendo, it takes place ninety-nine years before the first Lufia. That position gives the adventure a particular weight: it explores the people behind a history already introduced to players. Towns and turn-based battles supply a familiar framework, while the dungeons ask for observation and manipulation of the environment as well as a strong party.

cards.heading: A dungeon with moving parts
cards.text: Inside a dungeon, enemies are visible and respond to Maxim’s movement. Waiting gives the player time to consider a route; taking a step advances the situation. Tools such as arrows, bombs and a hookshot extend that relationship with the environment. An object may be part of a puzzle, a route may need opening, and a monster may be avoided or temporarily stopped. The result gives exploration its own decisions between battles, rather than treating every corridor as a pause before the next encounter.

cards.heading: What the party carries
cards.text: Equipment does more than increase statistics. Its IP abilities use a gauge built through taking damage, giving an older piece of gear a reason to remain useful after a stronger replacement appears. Capsule Monsters add another companion: these creatures fight under their own control and can develop when fed items or equipment. Together, these systems make preparation less automatic. The party’s strength comes from the tools and abilities it retains, and the player has to decide which combinations are worth carrying into the next dungeon.

main.title: Front Mission
main.summary: Front Mission is a tactical role-playing game developed by G-Craft and published by Square for the Super Famicom.

cards.text: Front Mission is a tactical role-playing game developed by G-Craft and published by Square for the Super Famicom. It was originally released only in Japan on February 24, 1995. Front Mission is the first main entry and the first entry overall in the Front Mission series. Front Mission is part of a serialized storyline that follows the stories of various characters and their struggles involving mecha known as wanzers. A direct port of the game was released for the WonderSwan Color in Japan on July 12, 2002.

A remake of the game developed by Square Enix Co., Ltd. was released for the PlayStation in Japan on October 23, 2003, titled Front Mission 1st. It included new content and offered a new USN scenario to play through. Front Mission 1st was then ported to the Nintendo DS with more additional content and was released in Japan on March 22, 2007. Only the Nintendo DS port, renamed as Front Mission, was released in North America on October 23, 2007.

A further remake of Front Mission 1st, titled Front Mission 1st: Remake, was developed and published by Forever Entertainment for the Nintendo Switch on November 30, 2022. Ports to PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Windows, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X/S were released on June 30, 2023.

main.title: Panzer Dragoon
main.subtitle: The world beneath a dragon’s wings
main.summary: Team Andromeda’s rail shooter pairs a dragon and rider with sweeping ruins, airborne machines and attacks arriving from every direction.

cards.heading: A rider in a ruined world
cards.text: Panzer Dragoon is Team Andromeda’s rail shooter, first released for Sega Saturn in Japan on 10 March 1995. A hunter becomes the rider of a blue dragon and pursues another dragon across the remains of an ancient civilisation. The flight follows a set route through three-dimensional environments, while the player moves the aiming reticle and shifts the dragon away from danger. Yukio Futatsugi directed the project, whose unfamiliar creatures, machinery and ruined landscapes gave one of Saturn’s early showcases a distinctive world of its own.

cards.heading: Looking behind the flight
cards.text: Enemies can arrive ahead, beside or behind the dragon. The player turns the view to face them, using the radar to notice threats outside the current screen. A quick press fires the rider’s gun; holding the button while passing the reticle over targets prepares the dragon’s homing lasers. Releasing it sends the locked shots outward. The difference gives each weapon a practical role: a small exposed target may reward a quick shot, while a group approaching from different angles invites a sweep of the reticle.

cards.heading: A landscape on a fixed route
cards.text: The predetermined flight lets each stage arrange a sequence of discoveries around the rider. Water, tunnels, ancient structures and huge airborne enemies come into view as the route advances, while the player continues aiming and dodging. Yoshitaka Azuma’s music accompanies that journey through a world whose history is also suggested by its surroundings. Jean Giraud, known as Moebius, illustrated the Japanese cover. The combination of a readable shooting system and a carefully presented setting established the series before Zwei expanded the flight and Saga changed its genre.

main.title: Chrono Trigger
main.subtitle: Time Becomes a Map to Traverse
main.summary: A fairground accident sends Crono across centuries, while combined attacks make the travelling party matter in battle.

cards.heading: A demonstration goes wrong
cards.text: Crono meets Marle at Guardia's Millennial Fair. They visit Lucca's Telepod demonstration, and a malfunction sends Marle into the past. Crono follows with her pendant. A public celebration becomes the doorway to a journey through different periods of the same planet, released by Square in 1995.

cards.heading: Time changes the company
cards.text: Prehistory, the medieval world and the distant future give the journey different surroundings and companions. The premise makes travelling through time a practical way of exploring a world. The collaboration brought together Dragon Quest creator Yuji Horii, Final Fantasy creators and Akira Toriyama's character designs.

cards.heading: Wait for the right combination
cards.text: In battle, action gauges fill while enemies change position. Characters can combine their special Tech abilities into joint attacks. Waiting for another party member can therefore create a different opportunity from acting immediately. The people travelling together affect both the story's company and the choices available during a fight.

cards.heading: The designers behind the Dream Team
cards.text: The game's development team included three designers that Square dubbed the "Dream Team": Hironobu Sakaguchi, creator of Square's Final Fantasy series; Yuji Horii, creator of Enix's Dragon Quest series; and Akira Toriyama, character designer of Dragon Quest and author of the Dragon Ball manga series. In addition, Takashi Tokita co-directed the game and co-wrote the scenario, Kazuhiko Aoki produced the game, while Masato Kato wrote most of the story.

features.title: Yasunori Mitsuda: choosing the sound first
features.summary: A score needs more than melodies.

cards.heading: Listen before writing notes
cards.text: Yasunori Mitsuda recalled beginning a Super Famicom working day by searching for sounds. With samplers such as the Akai S-3200 and E-MU EIII, he could spend hours listening through CDs before selecting material. Choosing a timbre was part of composing: it determined how a melody would sound through the console's limited playback hardware.

cards.heading: A demo addresses the musicians
cards.text: For later recording projects, Mitsuda chose sounds that would communicate the intended texture of a piece in its demo. Other specialists could adjust the final recording, but he wanted musicians to hear a convincing example before the session. The demo helped convey how the parts should combine and the weight or colour he expected from the performance.

cards.heading: The effects need a specialist
cards.text: When Mitsuda asked Hironobu Sakaguchi for composing work on Chrono Trigger, his previous sound-effects duties also needed to be reassigned. He contacted friends from school, including Yoshitaka Hirota, to help fill that role. Their conversations continued during development. The change allowed Mitsuda to concentrate on the score while other specialists produced the game's effects.

cards.heading: Different roles on different projects
cards.text: Mitsuda credited Minoru Akao alongside himself with improving the sound of Square's Super Famicom games. He continued to value sound programming as part of production. A later scheduling conflict changed his proposed composing role on Breath of Fire V into a production role, with Hitoshi Sakimoto writing the score and colleagues contributing sound work. His responsibilities could therefore vary considerably from one project to another.

main.title: Kirby's Dream Land 2
main.subtitle: Three friends change the journey
main.summary: The 1995 Game Boy sequel combines Kirby’s Copy Abilities with the talents of Rick, Kine and Coo, turning each partnership into a different way to explore.

cards.heading: Across the rainbow islands
cards.text: Kirby’s Dream Land 2 was released in Japan on March 21, 1995, developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo for Game Boy. The rainbow bridges connecting Dream Land’s islands have vanished. Kirby travels across seven islands to investigate, facing King Dedede’s followers and the threat of Dark Matter. This time the adventure includes Copy Abilities as well as three animal friends: Rick the hamster, Kine the fish and Coo the owl.

cards.heading: One ability, different partners
cards.text: Each companion changes how Kirby moves and how his copied power behaves. A familiar ability can therefore become a new tool when paired with another friend. The game turns the choice of travelling partner into part of exploration and combat, rather than just a change of appearance. Its original Game Boy music is credited collectively to Hirokazu Ando and Tadashi Ikegami; the small screen supports a broader range of partnerships without losing Kirby’s readable, direct actions.
